question.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(1,3)$ to the point $N(3,-1),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=3\,i-j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(3\,i-j-(i+3\,j)) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(2\,i-4\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3-4t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=3-4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i-4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+1-(3-4t)}(2+(-4))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{6t-2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{6t-2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{6(1)-2}-{e}^{6(0)-2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{6}}{3{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
